A fully managed service to create, publish, maintain, monitor, and secure APIs at any scale. It acts as the front door for clients to reach your backend services, whether serverless functions, HTTP endpoints, or AWS services.

Lambda
HTTP endpoints
AWS services

screens.title: What is Amazon API Gateway?
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon A P I Gateway is a fully managed service that acts as the front door for applications to access backend logic, data, or services. That claim means A P I Gateway accepts HTTP requests, applies policies and integrations you define, and returns responses while abstracting away server management. A useful mental model is to imagine A P I Gateway as a programmable proxy: it routes to Lambda functions for serverless operations, proxies to HTTP endpoints for traditional servers, or invokes AWS services directly when you want to avoid intermediate compute. This reduces operational burden because you no longer need to run and scale A P I servers or custom proxies. For example, in a serverless design you can expose a Lambda function that returns a greeting and let A P I Gateway handle authentication, logging, and throttling. One common misconception is thinking A P I Gateway merely forwards requests; in reality it also transforms payloads, enforces authorization, and caches responses. Another practical point is that A P I Gateway comes in three flavors—REST, HTTP, and WebSocket—so consider both feature needs and cost when choosing. As you proceed, ask yourself whether you need detailed request/response mapping or a lightweight proxy, because that choice influences which A P I type to pick.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: API Gateway is a managed API front door that routes requests to backends, enforces security, and offers optimizations like caching and transformations.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › What is Amazon API Gateway?
Definition & Analogy

API Gateway receives client calls, applies policies, and routes requests to backends such as Lambda, HTTP endpoints, or AWS services. Think of it as a programmable front door and traffic cop.

Why this matters
Reduces server management and centralizes cross-cutting concerns like auth and throttling.
Common misconception
API Gateway does more than proxying; it can transform payloads and enforce policies.
Concrete Example
Expose a Lambda function through API Gateway to serve a greeting to web clients. API Gateway handles the HTTP surface, auth, and metrics while Lambda runs the logic.
Key Takeaway

API Gateway centralizes routing, policy, and optimization so backend teams can focus on business logic.

screens.title: REST, HTTP, and WebSocket APIs
screens.narratorSegment: A P I Gateway supports three main A P I types, and choosing between them matters for cost, features, and behavior. REST APIs are the traditional, feature-rich option: they support full request/response transformations, custom authorizers, and detailed logging. Use REST APIs when you need VTL templating, advanced mapping, or fine-grained method configuration. HTTP APIs are a newer, lower-cost, and faster option that cover most simple request/response use cases, including proxying requests to Lambda or HTTP endpoints. If your needs are straightforward and you want lower latency and cost, HTTP APIs are often a good choice. WebSocket APIs enable persistent, two-way connections for real-time scenarios like chat, dashboards, or live gaming; they keep a connection open so messages can flow in both directions with low latency. A common misconception is to default to REST for everything; that can increase cost and complexity when an HTTP A P I would suffice. Conversely, using HTTP APIs when you require complex transformations or custom authorizers will leave you short on features. Think of REST as full-featured, HTTP as lean and fast, and WebSocket as the choice for persistent real-time communication.

keyIdea.text: REST = full features; HTTP = lower cost and better performance for simple APIs; WebSocket = real-time two-way communication.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › API Types

REST vs HTTP vs WebSocket

A side-by-side comparison to guide selection based on features and use case.

Comparison
REST API
Full features: request/response transformations, custom authorizers, detailed logging. Use for complex APIs and legacy integrations.
HTTP API
Lean and fast: lower cost, better performance for common proxying and Lambda-backed endpoints.
WebSocket API
Persistent two-way communication for chat, live dashboards, and gaming.
Example: simple API
A status endpoint that proxies to a Lambda often fits HTTP API.
Example: real-time
Chat requires WebSocket to maintain open connections and low latency message exchange.
Misconception check
Don’t always pick REST by default. Evaluate required features and cost. If you need VTL templates and custom authorizers you may need REST; otherwise HTTP may be preferable.
Key Takeaway

Match API type to needs: features vs cost vs latency vs persistent connection requirement.

screens.title: Integrations: Lambda, HTTP, AWS Services, Mock
screens.narratorSegment: Integrations define how A P I Gateway routes requests to your backend. The common types are Lambda integration, HTTP integration, AWS service integration, and mock integration. Lambda integration invokes a Lambda function and is the foundation for serverless APIs; A P I Gateway delivers the request payload to the function, and Lambda returns a response which A P I Gateway forwards to the client. HTTP integration proxies requests directly to public HTTP endpoints like an EC2-hosted service or an on-premises A P I. AWS service integration lets A P I Gateway call other services directly, for example publishing to Kinesis or sending messages to SQS, which avoids the need for an intermediate compute layer. Mock integration returns a response directly from A P I Gateway and is useful for testing or returning static responses during development. When designing integrations consider latency and cost: direct AWS service integrations reduce glue code, while Lambda introduces function execution time. Also understand that Lambda proxy integration simplifies mapping concerns by delivering the full request and expecting a formatted response. A practical example is exposing a /hello endpoint backed by a Lambda that reads query parameters and returns a JSON greeting. Think about which integration minimizes code and latency for your use case.

keyIdea.text: Choose Lambda for serverless logic, HTTP for proxying endpoints, AWS service integration to call services directly, and Mock for testing.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Integrations

Integration patterns

Define how API Gateway delivers requests to backends and returns responses to clients.

Lambda integration
API Gateway invokes a Lambda function and forwards its response. Use for serverless endpoints and when you want business logic in Lambda.
HTTP integration
Proxies to any public HTTP endpoint, useful when backend services run on EC2, on-premises, or external APIs.
AWS service integration
Call services like SQS or Kinesis directly from API Gateway to avoid intermediate compute.
Mock integration
Return a response without calling a backend. Useful for testing or static endpoints.
Concrete example
Expose a Lambda-backed /hello resource that reads a name from query string and returns a JSON greeting. This uses Lambda proxy integration so the function receives the full request context.
Why it matters

Selecting the right integration reduces code, latency, and cost while fitting operational constraints.

screens.title: Lambda Authorizer Example
screens.narratorSegment: Lambda authorizers let you provide custom authorization logic in a Lambda function that A P I Gateway invokes for each request. The simplified Python example in this chapter reads an authorizationToken from the event and decides Allow or Deny for the requested method. This pattern is flexible because you can validate JWTs, consult external identity providers, or check a database for permissions. The example uses a generate_policy helper to return the policy document that A P I Gateway expects. In practice you should replace the placeholder token checks with robust validation: cryptographic verification of JWTs, caching of validation results to reduce latency, and strict error handling for malformed input. A common misconception is thinking Lambda authorizers are free; they add latency and cost because they execute for each authorized request. Consider caching authorizer results where appropriate or using Cognito user pool authorizers when you only need standard JWT validation. Always ensure the authorizer returns the minimal allowed principal and adheres to least privilege. The code block shown is a starting point for custom logic and demonstrates the expected structure of the authorizer response.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Lambda Authorizer

Lambda Authorizer (Custom Authorizer)

A Lambda you provide that API Gateway invokes to authorize each request. Use it for custom token validation or third-party identity providers.

# Example Lambda Authorizer (Python)
import json

def lambda_handler(event, context):
  token = event['authorizationToken']
  method_arn = event['methodArn']

  # In a real scenario, validate the token (e.g., check JWT, database lookup)
  # For demonstration, let's say token "allow" grants access, "deny" denies
  if token == "allow":
    return generate_policy('user', 'Allow', method_arn)
  else:
    return generate_policy('user', 'Deny', method_arn)


def generate_policy(principal_id, effect, resource):
  auth_response = {
    'principalId': principal_id,
    'policyDocument': {
      'Version': '2012-10-17',
      'Statement': [
        {
          'Action': 'execute-api:Invoke',
          'Effect': effect,
          'Resource': resource
        }
      ]
    }
  }
  return auth_response
Guidance
Replace simple token checks with cryptographic validation of JWTs or external identity verification. Consider caching authorizer responses to reduce repeated validation cost.
Common pitfall

Running expensive external checks in the authorizer can add latency to every request; use cache where safe.

screens.title: Build a Serverless /hello Endpoint
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on process walks through creating a simple serverless REST A P I backed by a Python Lambda that returns a personalized greeting. Start by creating a Lambda function named myHelloFunction using Python. The function reads the incoming event to find a name either in query string parameters or in the JSON body, and returns a JSON response with a greeting. Next, create a REST A P I in A P I Gateway named MyHelloAPI and add a /hello resource. Configure a GET method on /hello using Lambda integration and enable Lambda proxy integration so the function receives the full request context. Save and deploy the A P I to a dev stage. This exercise teaches how A P I Gateway and Lambda work together, how proxy integration simplifies mapping, and how to verify behavior after deployment. As you complete it, reflect on where you might add auth, caching, or throttling.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Hands-on: /hello

Step-by-step

  1. Create Lambda function named myHelloFunction and grant basic Lambda permissions.
  2. Implement handler to read queryStringParameters and body for a name and return JSON.
  3. Create a REST API named MyHelloAPI and a resource /hello.
  4. Add GET method with Lambda integration and enable Lambda proxy integration.
  5. Deploy to a stage called dev and note the invoke URL for testing.
Starter code
import json

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    print(f"Received event: {json.dumps(event)}")
    name = "World"
    if event and 'queryStringParameters' in event and 'name' in event['queryStringParameters']:
        name = event['queryStringParameters']['name']
    elif event and 'body' in event:
        try:
            body_data = json.loads(event['body'])
            if 'name' in body_data:
                name = body_data['name']
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            pass

    message = f"Hello, {name}!"
    return {
        'statusCode': 200,
        'headers': {'Content-Type': 'application/json'},
        'body': json.dumps({'message': message})
    }
Try this

Invoke the deployed URL with ?name=YourName to confirm query parsing, or send a POST with JSON body containing name.

screens.title: Deploy, Test, and Validate Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: After wiring your Lambda to A P I Gateway and deploying a stage, testing is the critical next step. Get the invoke URL for the dev stage and call the endpoint in a browser or with curl. For example, call the URL with no parameters to verify the default greeting, then add a query string such as name=Cohortia to confirm the function reads queryStringParameters. If you added POST support, test sending JSON in the body and observe the returned message. Pay attention to response headers; when building web frontends you may need to enable CORS for browser requests to succeed. If you see generic 500 errors, examine CloudWatch logs for Lambda and A P I Gateway mapping templates; missing mapping or malformed JSON often leads to 500s. Also use A P I Gateway’s built-in test tool to simulate requests before deployment. Finally, consider adding simple smoke tests that call your endpoint after deployment to verify readiness. This testing loop ensures your A P I behaves correctly across query strings, request bodies, and potential error paths, and it surfaces common issues like missing permissions or CORS early in development.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Deploy & Test

Deployment & Validation Steps

  1. Deploy API to a stage (for example, dev) and record the invoke URL.
  2. Test with a browser: InvokeURL/hello and InvokeURL/hello?name=Cohortia.
  3. Use curl to simulate different client behaviors and observe headers and status codes.
  4. If you get 500s, inspect CloudWatch logs for Lambda and API Gateway to find mapping or runtime errors.
  5. Enable CORS for browser-based frontends and retest to avoid cross-origin errors.
Quick commands
Use curl to test endpoints and include query strings or JSON bodies. Also use API Gateway’s console test tool to exercise method mapping without external traffic.
Pitfall

Forgetting to enable CORS or to grant API Gateway permission to invoke your Lambda are frequent causes of failed tests.

screens.title: Caching, Throttling, and Transformations
screens.narratorSegment: A P I Gateway provides a set of operational features that improve performance and protect your backends. Caching lets A P I Gateway store responses for a configured TTL, so repeated requests can be served from cache without invoking the backend. This reduces latency and Lambda invocations for frequently requested data. A crucial consideration with caching is data freshness: cached entries become stale unless you invalidate them or use short TTLs when data changes frequently. Throttling protects your backend from sudden spikes by imposing request limits and burst settings either globally or per method. Configure throttling to avoid overloading services and use burst limits to tolerate short peaks. Request and response transformations, powered by VTL templates in REST APIs, let you adapt payload schemas to match legacy services or to strip unnecessary fields before hitting the backend. This is especially useful when integrating with older systems that expect different JSON shapes. A common mistake is enabling caching without a clear invalidation strategy; pair caching with a plan to refresh or evict stale entries. Together these features help you balance cost, performance, and correctness in production APIs.

narration.text: A P I Gateway provides a set of operational features that improve performance and protect your backends. Caching lets A P I Gateway store responses for a configured TTL, so repeated requests can be served from cache without invoking the backend. This reduces latency and Lambda invocations for frequently requested data. A crucial consideration with caching is data freshness: cached entries become stale unless you invalidate them or use short TTLs when data changes frequently. Throttling protects your backend from sudden spikes by imposing request limits and burst settings either globally or per method. Configure throttling to avoid overloading services and use burst limits to tolerate short peaks. Request and response transformations, powered by VTL templates in REST APIs, let you adapt payload schemas to match legacy services or to strip unnecessary fields before hitting the backend. This is especially useful when integrating with older systems that expect different JSON shapes. A common mistake is enabling caching without a clear invalidation strategy; pair caching with a plan to refresh or evict stale entries. Together these features help you balance cost, performance, and correctness in production APIs.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Caching & Throttling

Performance & Resilience Features

Caching
Cache responses at API Gateway with a TTL to reduce backend load. Plan for invalidation to avoid stale data.
Throttling
Set global or per-method rate and burst limits to protect your backend from overload.
Transformations
Use VTL in REST APIs to transform requests or responses when integrating with legacy systems.
Consider using caching for read-heavy endpoints where data does not change frequently. For endpoints that must reflect real-time updates, opt for short TTLs or avoid caching. Use throttling to avoid cascading failures and design graceful error handling for clients when limits are hit.
Example
A GET /products endpoint can be cached for 60 seconds to reduce Lambda calls for frequent reads, but invalidate after product updates.
Key Takeaway

Use caching and throttling thoughtfully; pair caching with invalidation strategies to ensure correct responses.

screens.title: Authorization Mechanisms
screens.narratorSegment: A P I Gateway supports several authorization mechanisms and you should pick the one that matches your trust model and clients. IAM authorizers use IAM roles and policies and are ideal for service-to-service access when callers are other AWS services or trusted machines; they enforce least privilege via IAM. Lambda authorizers run a custom Lambda to return an allow/deny policy; they are highly flexible and allow integration with third-party identity providers or complex checks. Cognito User Pool authorizers validate JWT tokens issued by Cognito, making them a straightforward choice for user-facing applications that rely on Cognito for authentication. Each mechanism has tradeoffs: IAM is powerful for internal access and leverages existing AWS identities, Lambda authorizers offer custom logic but add latency and cost per request, and Cognito authorizers simplify common authentication flows but require using Cognito for user management. When designing security, always apply the principle of least privilege: grant A P I Gateway and backends only the permissions they need. Also think about token lifetimes and caching authorizer results to reduce repeated validation overhead. Choosing the wrong authorizer can cause unnecessary complexity or performance impacts, so map your access patterns before deciding.

Authorization options

IAM Authorizer
Use IAM roles and policies. Best for service-to-service access and internal apps.
Lambda Authorizer
Custom logic in a Lambda. Flexible but adds latency and cost per request.
Cognito User Pool
Validates JWT tokens issued by Cognito, ideal for user-facing apps using Cognito for auth.
Map your clients and trust model to an authorizer: internal AWS callers often fit IAM, public web users fit Cognito or Lambda authorizers, and third-party identity providers often require a Lambda authorizer to validate tokens.

screens.title: CORS, Error Mapping, and Least Privilege
screens.narratorSegment: Several common mistakes surface repeatedly when teams adopt A P I Gateway. First, CORS errors are frequent when a browser-based frontend calls an A P I deployed on a different domain. You must explicitly enable CORS for the relevant methods in A P I Gateway; otherwise the browser will block responses even if the A P I returns valid data. Second, error handling and mapping templates matter: if you do not map backend errors into meaningful client responses, clients may receive opaque 500 errors that make debugging hard. Use mapping templates to normalize error shapes and HTTP status codes. Third, least privilege is essential: grant A P I Gateway and any backend Lambda only the permissions they need. Overly broad IAM policies can expose services to misuse. Fourth, private backends require a VPC Link for private integrations so traffic does not traverse the public internet. A common misconception is that default settings are safe; take the time to configure CORS, error mappings, and IAM roles deliberately. Each of these fixes prevents production surprises and improves client and developer experience. CORS, Error Mapping, and Least Privilege means enable cors, map backend errors clearly, apply least privilege, and use vpc link for private integrations to avoid common failures.. In practical terms, avoid common mistakes that break client behavior or create security risks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Troubles to watch for

CORS errors
Browsers block cross-origin requests unless CORS is explicitly enabled for methods and origins.
Error mapping
Without mapping templates clients may receive generic 500s; normalize error payloads for clarity.
Least privilege
Grant only necessary permissions to Lambdas and API Gateway roles to reduce security risk.

Use VPC Link to integrate with private resources in your VPC and avoid public internet traversal.

Create usage plans to assign quotas and throttling to API keys for specific consumers. This helps manage partner access and support monetization models.

Define request quotas per period to limit overall consumption.

Combine usage plans with throttling to prevent abuse and protect backends.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore Amazon A P I Gateway, a fully managed front door for your application logic. You will learn what A P I Gateway does, why it matters for serverless and traditional architectures, and how to choose between REST, HTTP, and WebSocket APIs. A P I Gateway handles routing, integrations, authorization, caching, throttling, and transformations so developers can focus on business logic instead of running and scaling A P I infrastructure. For example, you can expose an AWS Lambda function through A P I Gateway to serve a simple greeting endpoint without running servers. We will also cover how A P I Gateway integrates directly with AWS services, how to secure endpoints with IAM, Lambda authorizers, or Cognito, and when to enable caching or throttling to protect your backend. By the end of this chapter you will understand the role A P I Gateway plays in production systems, common pitfalls such as CORS and stale caches, and concrete steps to create a serverless A P I and deploy it to a stage. Think about a simple web app that needs a single endpoint: A P I Gateway lets you expose that endpoint securely and scale it automatically. What A P I type would your app need, and why?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the role of Amazon A P I Gateway as a fully managed A P I front door, choose the correct A P I type for a given use case, configure integrations to Lambda, HTTP, or other AWS services, and implement authorization to secure endpoints. Each objective maps to practical skills: you will describe why A P I Gateway matters in serverless and traditional stacks, differentiate REST, HTTP, and WebSocket APIs and when to use each, wire integrations that route requests to Lambda or other services and understand mock responses for testing, and apply IAM roles, Cognito user pools, or Lambda authorizers to control access. These are not just definitions: you will also practice deploying a simple serverless endpoint and verifying behavior, think through cache TTL and invalidation questions, and design throttling limits to protect backends. Finally you will be able to reason about common pitfalls like CORS and stale caches so your clients and backends communicate reliably. Consider how these competencies map to a production A P I: the ability to pick the right A P I type and secure it correctly makes your service more maintainable, scalable, and safer.

These objectives map directly to practical activities. You will deploy a simple Python Lambda, connect it to A P I Gateway, and verify responses for query string and body parameters. You will practice setting up method-level authorization and observe what changes when you switch from an IAM policy to a Cognito user pool. You will also enable caching and measure the difference in backend invocations, and configure throttling to protect your Lambda from sudden bursts. Each skill helps you reason about real production tradeoffs: when low latency and low cost favor HTTP APIs, when complex request/response mapping needs REST APIs, and when persistent two-way communication requires WebSocket. The hands-on activity included in this chapter walks through creating a /hello resource, deploying to a dev stage, and testing with query parameters to confirm correct behavior. After completing it, you will be able to answer architecture questions like which A P I type suits a chat application and which features to turn on for frequently read but rarely changed data. These practical checks ensure you not only understand concepts but can apply them.

Amazon A P I Gateway is a fully managed service that acts as the front door for applications to access backend logic, data, or services. That claim means A P I Gateway accepts HTTP requests, applies policies and integrations you define, and returns responses while abstracting away server management. A useful mental model is to imagine A P I Gateway as a programmable proxy: it routes to Lambda functions for serverless operations, proxies to HTTP endpoints for traditional servers, or invokes AWS services directly when you want to avoid intermediate compute. This reduces operational burden because you no longer need to run and scale A P I servers or custom proxies. For example, in a serverless design you can expose a Lambda function that returns a greeting and let A P I Gateway handle authentication, logging, and throttling. One common misconception is thinking A P I Gateway merely forwards requests; in reality it also transforms payloads, enforces authorization, and caches responses. Another practical point is that A P I Gateway comes in three flavors—REST, HTTP, and WebSocket—so consider both feature needs and cost when choosing. As you proceed, ask yourself whether you need detailed request/response mapping or a lightweight proxy, because that choice influences which A P I type to pick.

A P I Gateway supports three main A P I types, and choosing between them matters for cost, features, and behavior. REST APIs are the traditional, feature-rich option: they support full request/response transformations, custom authorizers, and detailed logging. Use REST APIs when you need VTL templating, advanced mapping, or fine-grained method configuration. HTTP APIs are a newer, lower-cost, and faster option that cover most simple request/response use cases, including proxying requests to Lambda or HTTP endpoints. If your needs are straightforward and you want lower latency and cost, HTTP APIs are often a good choice. WebSocket APIs enable persistent, two-way connections for real-time scenarios like chat, dashboards, or live gaming; they keep a connection open so messages can flow in both directions with low latency. A common misconception is to default to REST for everything; that can increase cost and complexity when an HTTP A P I would suffice. Conversely, using HTTP APIs when you require complex transformations or custom authorizers will leave you short on features. Think of REST as full-featured, HTTP as lean and fast, and WebSocket as the choice for persistent real-time communication.

Integrations define how A P I Gateway routes requests to your backend. The common types are Lambda integration, HTTP integration, AWS service integration, and mock integration. Lambda integration invokes a Lambda function and is the foundation for serverless APIs; A P I Gateway delivers the request payload to the function, and Lambda returns a response which A P I Gateway forwards to the client. HTTP integration proxies requests directly to public HTTP endpoints like an EC2-hosted service or an on-premises A P I. AWS service integration lets A P I Gateway call other services directly, for example publishing to Kinesis or sending messages to SQS, which avoids the need for an intermediate compute layer. Mock integration returns a response directly from A P I Gateway and is useful for testing or returning static responses during development. When designing integrations consider latency and cost: direct AWS service integrations reduce glue code, while Lambda introduces function execution time. Also understand that Lambda proxy integration simplifies mapping concerns by delivering the full request and expecting a formatted response. A practical example is exposing a /hello endpoint backed by a Lambda that reads query parameters and returns a JSON greeting. Think about which integration minimizes code and latency for your use case.

Lambda authorizers let you provide custom authorization logic in a Lambda function that A P I Gateway invokes for each request. The simplified Python example in this chapter reads an authorizationToken from the event and decides Allow or Deny for the requested method. This pattern is flexible because you can validate JWTs, consult external identity providers, or check a database for permissions. The example uses a generate_policy helper to return the policy document that A P I Gateway expects. In practice you should replace the placeholder token checks with robust validation: cryptographic verification of JWTs, caching of validation results to reduce latency, and strict error handling for malformed input. A common misconception is thinking Lambda authorizers are free; they add latency and cost because they execute for each authorized request. Consider caching authorizer results where appropriate or using Cognito user pool authorizers when you only need standard JWT validation. Always ensure the authorizer returns the minimal allowed principal and adheres to least privilege. The code block shown is a starting point for custom logic and demonstrates the expected structure of the authorizer response.

This hands-on process walks through creating a simple serverless REST A P I backed by a Python Lambda that returns a personalized greeting. Start by creating a Lambda function named myHelloFunction using Python.
